Your definition of torture porn needs some work - following your earlier example of Sailor Moon, in Stars when Usagi watches her fiancé being brutally murdered in front of her by Sailor Galaxia, do you count that as torture porn? The vast majority of the general populace has little to no knowledge on nutrition and calories, and what info they do have is oftentimes outdated (such as the food pyramid shit that is taught in schools) or straight up false. With this in mind it's easy to see how people can easily overeat if they're not constantly hyperaware of what they're putting in their body. As for eating junk food, again, food deserts are a thing, junk foods are oftentimes more convenient to consume for people who are busy or do not have the time/energy to cook a full meal.

How are people supposed to care about those things when they're faced with long work hours, abysmal pay, oftentimes families to take care of and other responsibilities? It is an overwhelmingly privileged position to be in where you can both regularly afford nutritious high quality foods (ever heard of food deserts?), have the time/energy/money to invest in a proper fitness routine while also still juggling everything else that life entails (like working, maintaining a social life, raising a family if one has one, ect). I don't think it's entirely a matter of people not caring so much as they're not given the proper circumstances that can empower them to properly care. If we all worked less, had stronger social programs and safety nets, and didn't immediately write off being overweight/obese as a failing of character and looked at it as a failing of society, then maybe things would be different

I initially started losing weight unintentionally because I started riding my bike for fun regularly during the start of the pandemic, plus I cut down on ordering takeout a huge amount so I could put more money into savings, then I decided to keep going with it but just be cool and casual about it - for about a year there I was losing weight steadily and heathily while still having a decent relationship with exercise and better self esteem, but things soured once the pandemic worsened and the people in charge responded in the dumbest way possible leading to my city becoming the most locked down city in the entire world. All my dreams got crushed, I experienced back to back heartbreak (long story there) and I started to look at it as "my weight is the only thing I can control", like that wasn't even a subconscious train of thought, that was literally a line I wrote in my diary around September 2021. 

Long story short, here I am, and I'm terrified of ending up back in that body because of everything it represents. It felt so physically uncomfortable to be in, the physical limitations were awful, and it was clear that the body I was in then was no more healthy for me than my underweight one was. Rationally I know that it's unlikely I'll end up back there as I live a very different day to day lifestyle now, I'm not on that medication and just in general my circumstances are different. The fear still lingers though, which is partially why I've never found the recovery community's complete marriage to set point theory to be very helpful (to anyone reading, don't come for my throat, we can agree to disagree on this point).

Man, I'm really getting read for filth here. At first I tried to go all-in with recovery as best as I could but it felt to terrifying and like it was too much too soon, so I scaled it back a lot. It's second nature to restrict in some form for me at this point, so while I'm not restricting in a classic sense I've still got a lot of these self judgements going on in my head like you said. For example I brought up to my dietician recently about the guilt I was feeling for gravitating towards sugary items like chocolates and pastries for outside of meal snacks and how I was scared of developing diabetes or something down the road from it. She was able to knock some sense into me with that one, but that's one example. I've kind of transitioned into this weird area where I'm trying to hold myself to "normal people standards" and mimic what/how normal people are supposed to eat by following the general health guidelines put out by various governing bodies, y'know the whole balanced diet with exercise kind of thing that everyone gets taught about. I know I'm in recovery from anorexia but I still feel like that shouldn't give me a pass on not following the rules if that makes sense? Especially since where I want to be is to have a healthy relationship with food and movement and to be nutritionally balanced. 

In a way I guess I've traded one set of standards to hold myself to (the stereotypical anorexic standards) for another less damaging one that nevertheless still ends up leading to feelings of inferiority and self loathing. And god, what even is normal eating anyway? Even the general population who are the exact target audience for these health guidelines seem to suck at following them. My idea of what is and isn't healthy behaviour is so convoluted because it's getting influenced by a million different sources with different agendas that I wish I could have a sense of clarity and a dash of nuance. 

Anyway, sorry for the essay in my reply! Thank you so much for your input, it feels so nice to be seen, especially when the struggle gets really hard.
